cta.p: When care can't bring a garment back to compliance, replace it — certified hi-vis and weatherproofs from stock, with embroidery for teams.

pages.cardBlurb: Wash limits, tape damage and the point where a faded garment stops being compliant.
pages.h1: Caring for hi-vis: wash limits & compliance.
pages.metaTitle: Caring for Hi-Vis: Wash Limits, Fading & Compliance | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Hi-vis carries a maximum wash count and its certification dies with the colour — how to wash it, what ruins tape and fluoro, and when a faded garment must be retired.
pages.lede: A hi-vis vest is the only garment in the wash basket with an expiry counter printed on the label. EN ISO 20471 certification is tested up to a maximum number of washes — past that count, or past a certain amount of fading, the garment is workwear-shaped but no longer hi-vis in law.

steps.name: Check the wash count on the label
steps.text: Next to the care symbols is a maximum number of wash cycles — commonly 25. The garment's certification was tested to that count; keep rough track, especially on kit washed weekly.

steps.name: Close fastenings and turn inside out
steps.text: Velcro is the number-one shredder of retroreflective tape in a drum. Close every strip, zip the zips, turn the garment inside out.

steps.name: Wash cool on a gentle cycle
steps.text: Follow the label temperature — typically 40 °C or below. No bleach, no fabric softener, no optical-brightener detergents: all three coat or strip the fluorescent dye and dull the tape.

steps.name: Dry on the line, iron never near the tape
steps.text: Line-dry or tumble cool if the label allows. Direct iron contact melts retroreflective tape on contact — if you must press the fabric, keep the iron off the tape entirely.

steps.name: Inspect against daylight before it goes back on
steps.text: Fluoro should still look electric next to a new garment; tape should be intact and mirror-bright. Grey-tinged fabric, cracked or peeling tape, rips or heavy oil staining mean retirement.

blocks.h2: You're washing the certification, not just the garment
blocks.html:
High-visibility clothing earns its EN ISO 20471 badge with two materials: fluorescent background fabric that reacts with daylight, and retroreflective tape that returns headlight beams. Both are consumables. Every wash, every month of UV, every scrape takes a little performance off each — and the standard certifies the garment only up to a stated number of care cycles.

That's why hi-vis care is different from ordinary laundry: the goal isn't keeping it looking nice, it's keeping it legally conspicuous. The routine below protects both materials; the checklist after it tells you when protection has run out.

items.h3: Find the wash count on the label
items.html: Alongside the care icons is a maximum wash-cycle number — 25 is typical, some heavier garments carry 50. Certification was tested at that count. For kit washed every week, that's an expiry measured in months — keep rough track.

items.h3: Close every fastening, turn it inside out
items.html: Open velcro in a drum shreds retroreflective tape faster than anything else on this page. Close the strips, zip up, turn inside out so the tape rides against the garment's own lining.

Wash at the label temperature — usually 40 °C or lower — on a gentle cycle. Skip bleach, fabric softener and "whiter-than-white" detergents with optical brighteners: they strip fluorescent dye or leave films that dull both fabric and tape.

items.h3: Line-dry; keep irons away from tape
items.html: Heat is the enemy of tape adhesive and fluoro dye alike. Line-dry where possible, tumble only cool and only if the label allows, and never run an iron over retroreflective strips.
Hold it next to a newer garment outdoors. The background should still jump out; the tape should be unbroken and brilliant. If either fails the eye test, it fails the road test.

blocks.lead: Each of these is a compliance failure, not a cosmetic one.
head: What you see
Why it fails
Verdict
rows: Fluoro faded toward grey or pastel
Below the standard's colour performance — invisible by day
Past the label's max wash count
Certification tested only to that count
Minimum visible area no longer met
Oil or paint staining that won't wash out
Stains mask fluorescence exactly where it's needed

blocks.html: A faded vest is worse than no vest — it changes the wearer's behaviour ("I'm wearing hi-vis") without changing what the driver sees. If a garment wouldn't pass the side-by-side daylight comparison against new stock, take it off the van.
Not sure which class you should be replacing it with? Class 2 vs Class 3 — which do you need? → Or start at the hi-vis hub.

faq.q: How many times can you wash hi-vis?
faq.a: Check the garment label — EN ISO 20471 certification is tested to a stated maximum number of wash cycles, commonly 25. Beyond that count the garment's performance is no longer certified, even if it still looks reasonable.

faq.q: Why can't you use fabric softener on hi-vis?
faq.a: Softener leaves a film that dulls the fluorescent dye and coats the retroreflective tape, cutting both daytime and night-time performance. Bleach and optical-brightener detergents damage the dye directly. Plain detergent, cool wash, gentle cycle.

faq.q: When should a hi-vis vest be replaced?
faq.a: When the fluorescent colour has visibly faded toward grey, the tape is cracked, peeling or dull, the garment is ripped or heavily stained, or it has passed the wash count on its label. Any one of those alone is enough — the certification depends on all of them holding.

faq.q: Can you tumble-dry hi-vis?
faq.a: Only if the label allows it, and then only on a cool setting. Heat degrades both the fluorescent dye and the adhesive bonding the retroreflective tape, so line-drying is the safer default — and never iron over the tape.

pages.cardBlurb: Why jackets "leak" when the membrane is fine, and the wash-in fix that restores the beading.
pages.h1: Reproofing waterproofs: bring the beading back.
pages.metaTitle: Reproofing Waterproof Jackets: DWR, Wetting Out & EN 343 | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Most "leaking" waterproofs have a worn DWR coating, not a failed membrane — how to tell, how to wash and reproof the jacket, and when it genuinely is dead.
pages.lede: Nine "leaking" work jackets out of ten haven't failed — their invisible outer coating has. When rain stops beading and the face fabric soaks dark, the fix is a washing machine and a bottle of reproofer, not a replacement. Here's the diagnosis, the fix, and the honest signs a jacket really is done.

steps.name: Diagnose: wet face fabric or wet inside?
steps.text: Fabric soaking dark and feeling heavy is wetting-out — worn DWR, fixable. Water pooling inside along seams or through the body with the outer merely damp points at seams or membrane.

steps.name: Wash the jacket clean first
steps.text: Dirt and body oils are what killed the DWR. Wash per the label with pure soap or a technical cleaner — never softener or bio detergent — and rinse twice.

steps.name: Apply a wash-in reproofer
steps.text: Run a second cycle with a wash-in DWR treatment, dosed per the bottle. Spray-on products suit garments with wicking liners you don't want coated.

steps.name: Heat-activate if the label allows
steps.text: Most reproofers cure with gentle heat — a cool tumble cycle or a warm iron over a cloth, per the garment label. Skip this only if the label forbids all heat.

steps.name: Test and repeat seasonally
steps.text: Sprinkle water on the sleeve: it should bead and roll. Plan on reproofing once or twice a year for daily-wear outdoor kit — sooner whenever beading stops.

blocks.html:
A waterproof work jacket keeps rain out with a membrane or coating bonded inside the fabric. But it stays comfortable thanks to something else: a DWR (durable water repellent) finish on the outer face that makes rain bead up and roll off.

DWR wears away — abraded by straps and tool belts, clogged by mud and body oils, stripped by harsh detergents. When it goes, the face fabric drinks water and the jacket feels like it's leaking: heavy, cold and clammy, because the soaked outer kills breathability and chills you through. The membrane underneath is usually still doing its job.

That distinction decides everything. Wet, dark, heavy face fabric = wetting out — restore the DWR and the jacket comes back. Water genuinely pooling inside while the outer stays merely damp — that's seams or membrane, and reproofing won't help.

items.html: Sprinkle water on the shoulder. If it soaks flat into the fabric instead of beading, the DWR is gone. If it beads but you're still getting wet inside, jump to the last section — the problem is elsewhere.

Reproofer bonds to clean fibre, and the dirt is half the problem anyway. Wash per the care label with a technical cleaner or pure soap. No fabric softener, no bio detergent — both strip or block DWR. Rinse twice to clear residue.

Wash-in DWR treatments go in the drawer for a second cycle, dosed per the bottle. Use spray-on instead if the jacket has a wicking mesh liner you don't want coated — spray the outer only, evenly, while damp.
Most treatments need warmth to bond: a cool tumble-dry or a warm iron over a tea towel, whichever the garment label permits. This step is where most home reproofing jobs succeed or fail.
Water on the sleeve should sit up in beads and roll. For a jacket worn daily outdoors, expect to repeat once or twice a year — the trigger is beading stopping, not the calendar.

blocks.h2: What EN 343 tells you on the label

items.l: First figure: resistance to water penetration, class 1–4 — higher survives heavier, longer rain
Second figure: breathability, class 1–4 — higher moves sweat out faster
A 4:1 keeps rain out but boils you; daily outdoor work wants both figures healthy

blocks.lead: DWR restores the outer. These failures are structural.
head: Symptom
What's failed
Verdict
rows: Wet lines inside along the seams
Inner coating peeling, flaking or sticky
Leaks at the zip in driving rain
Zip or storm flap worn out
Repair if the jacket merits it
Face fabric abraded past holding DWR

blocks.html: Hi-vis waterproofs: check the wash count too. A hi-vis rain jacket is certified under EN ISO 20471 as well as EN 343 — it carries a maximum wash-cycle rating, and every cleaning-and-reproofing round counts against it. Care rules for the fluoro and tape are covered in caring for hi-vis.

faq.q: Why does my waterproof jacket soak through but not leak?
faq.a: That's wetting out: the DWR coating on the face fabric has worn off, so the outer soaks up water and feels cold and clammy even though the membrane inside is still waterproof. Washing the jacket clean and applying a wash-in reproofer restores it.

faq.q: How often should you reproof a work jacket?
faq.a: When water stops beading on the surface — for daily outdoor wear that's typically once or twice a year. Always wash the jacket clean first; reproofer over dirt and body oils won't bond.

faq.q: Can you use normal detergent on waterproof jackets?
faq.a: Avoid biological detergents and never use fabric softener — both degrade the DWR finish and can affect the membrane's performance. Use a technical cleaner or pure soap, rinse thoroughly, and reproof after washing if beading has stopped.

faq.q: What do the EN 343 numbers on a jacket mean?
faq.a: Two classes, each 1–4: the first is resistance to water penetration, the second is breathability. Higher is better in both. A jacket rated 4:4 is the top spec; a high first number with a low second keeps rain out but traps sweat.

pages.cardBlurb: Why hydrocarbons laugh at a normal wash, the pre-treat routine that works, and why it's a safety job on FR kit.
pages.h1: Getting oil & grease out of workwear.
pages.metaTitle: Oil & Grease Out of Workwear: What Actually Works | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Why oil survives a normal wash cycle, the pre-treat-then-hot-wash routine that shifts it, and why oil removal is a safety requirement — not a cosmetic one — on FR garments.
pages.lede: Oil beats an ordinary wash for a simple reason: it isn't water-soluble, and a 40-degree cycle with everyday detergent mostly just spreads it around. Getting it out is a two-step job — dissolve first, then wash hot. And on flame-resistant kit, it isn't optional.

steps.name: Scrape and blot fresh contamination
steps.text: Lift what sits on the surface with a blunt edge and blot with paper or rag. Don't rub it deeper into the weave.

steps.name: Pre-treat while the stain is fresh
steps.text: Work a solvent-based degreaser or neat washing-up liquid into the mark and give it 15–30 minutes. This step dissolves what the wash alone can't.

steps.name: Wash hot, per the label, with a heavy-duty detergent
steps.text: Use the hottest cycle the care label allows and don't overload the drum. Heavy-duty liquid detergents carry the surfactant load that oils need.

steps.name: Check before it dries
steps.text: Air-dry and inspect. Heat-drying a garment with oil still in it sets the stain — and on any garment, repeat treatment beats a tumble-dried mistake.

steps.name: Repeat once — then make the call
steps.text: A second pre-treat-and-hot-wash shifts most survivors. What remains after that is in the fibre for good: cosmetic on a polo, disqualifying on FR kit.

blocks.h2: Oil doesn't dissolve in water — so the wash needs help
blocks.html:
Detergents bridge oil and water, but an everyday low-temperature cycle gives them too little to work with: not enough heat to soften the grease, not enough chemistry to dissolve it. The fix isn't a stronger machine — it's pre-treatment: getting a degreasing agent into the stain before the wash, so the cycle has something it can actually rinse away.

Speed matters more than product choice. Fresh oil sits in the weave; week-old oil has oxidised into it. The crews whose kit stays presentable treat marks at the end of the shift, not at the end of the month.

items.html: Lift surface grease with a blunt edge and blot with rag or paper. Rubbing drives oil deeper and spreads the mark.
Work a solvent-based degreaser (or neat washing-up liquid — it's a kitchen-grade degreaser) into the stain. Leave it 15–30 minutes to dissolve the oil. Skipping this step is why the stain survives.
The hottest cycle the care label allows, a heavy-duty liquid detergent, and room in the drum for the garment to move. Cold cycles preserve oil beautifully.
Tumble heat sets any oil still in the fabric. Check clean before any heat drying — if in doubt, line-dry.
Run the pre-treat and hot wash once more if needed. Still marked after two rounds? On uniform kit that's cosmetic. On FR kit, see below — it's retirement.

blocks.html: On FR garments, oil removal is a safety requirement. A flame-resistant coverall soaked with hydrocarbons can ignite and burn regardless of its rating — the fuel is in the fabric. Oily FR kit comes off shift for proper laundering, and a garment that won't come clean is retired, not tolerated. The full washing rules are in the FR wash guide.

blocks.h2: Shift it, live with it, or retire it
head: Situation
Verdict
rows: Fresh oil on poly-cotton polos, trousers, coveralls
Shifts — pre-treat + hot wash, usually first time
Old, oxidised staining on uniform kit
Cosmetic — fabric is clean after washing even if shadowed; demote to dirty-work kit if looks matter
Any oil saturation on FR / arc / antistatic kit
Launder properly or retire — contamination defeats the protection
Oil on hi-vis fluorescent panels that won't lift
Retire — stains mask fluorescence where it's measured

faq.q: How do you get engine oil out of work clothes?
faq.a: Blot off the surface oil, pre-treat with a degreaser or neat washing-up liquid for 15–30 minutes, then wash on the hottest cycle the care label allows with a heavy-duty detergent. Air-dry and check before tumble-drying — heat sets any oil left in the fabric.

faq.q: Why won't oil come out in a normal wash?
faq.a: Oil isn't water-soluble, and a cool cycle with everyday detergent lacks both the heat and the chemistry to dissolve it. Without pre-treatment the wash mostly redistributes the oil — which is why the mark 'survives' laundering.

faq.q: Is it safe to wear oil-stained FR workwear?
faq.a: No. Hydrocarbon contamination makes flame-resistant fabric ignitable regardless of its certified rating — the oil is fuel held against your body. Oily FR garments need proper laundering before reuse, and kit that won't come clean gets retired.

faq.q: Does washing-up liquid really work on oil stains?
faq.a: Yes — it's formulated to cut kitchen grease and works the same way on workshop oil as a pre-treatment. Work it in neat, wait 20 minutes, then machine wash hot. For heavy or repeated contamination a purpose-made solvent degreaser is stronger.

pages.cardBlurb: Keeping stitched logos sharp and printed ones attached through hundreds of industrial washes.
pages.metaTitle: Washing Embroidered & Printed Workwear Properly | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to launder branded workwear so stitched logos stay sharp and printed ones stay attached — inside-out washing, temperature rules, and why print and embroidery age differently.
pages.lede: A logo is the hardest-working part of a uniform: it goes through every wash the garment does, and it fails in public. Embroidery and print age differently — stitching frays and puckers, print cracks and peels — but the laundering habits that protect them are nearly identical.

heroMeta.l: The one habit that matters most

steps.name: Close fastenings and turn inside out
steps.text: Drum abrasion is what dulls embroidery and cracks print. Inside out, the garment's own fabric takes the friction instead of the decoration.

steps.name: Wash at 40 °C on a normal cycle
steps.text: Hot enough for workwear soil, cool enough for rayon threads and transfer adhesives. Go hotter only if both garment and decoration specs allow it.

steps.name: Use standard detergent — skip bleach and softener
steps.text: Bleach strips thread colour; softener coats print and helps it lift at the edges.

steps.name: Line-dry or tumble cool
steps.text: High tumble heat is the number-one killer of heat-applied transfers and shrinks stitched areas into puckering.

steps.name: Iron around, never across
steps.text: If pressing is needed, iron the fabric around the decoration, or press on the reverse with a cloth over embroidery. A hot plate directly on print re-melts it.

blocks.html:
Embroidery is thousands of thread stitches through a stabilised patch of fabric. It fails by abrasion and heat: threads dull and fuzz where the drum grinds them, and aggressive drying shrinks the fabric behind the stitches so the logo puckers. It is, however, the tougher of the two — which is why it's the default for kit washed constantly.

Printed and heat-transferred logos are a film bonded to the fabric surface. They fail by heat and flexing: hot washes and hot tumbles soften the adhesive, edges lift, and the film cracks along fold lines. Print earns its place on garments where stitching doesn't work — waterproof shells (needle holes compromise membranes) and large-format designs.

Same protective habits either way — the routine below — plus one purchasing note: on hi-vis and FR kit, decoration placement and process affect certification, so brand through your supplier rather than a high-street press.

blocks.h2: Five habits that keep logos sharp

items.html: The single highest-value habit: the drum abrades the garment's inside instead of the logo. Velcro closed — it grabs threads and transfer edges alike.
The branded-kit compromise: hot enough for real soil, gentle enough for threads and adhesives. Check both the garment label and the decoration spec before going hotter.
Bleach takes the colour out of thread; softener leaves a film that lifts print edges and dulls stitching. Standard detergent does the job.
Hot tumbling is the top cause of peeled transfers. Line-dry where possible; tumble low where not.
Never run a hot plate across a printed logo — it re-melts. Press around decorations, or on the reverse through a cloth for embroidered areas.

blocks.h2: Embroidery or print — decided by the garment
head: Garment
Better choice
Why
rows: Survives hundreds of washes; premium look
Decoration must not cover certified fluoro or tape areas
Threads, films and processes must be FR-compatible
Embroidery at that scale is heavy and stiff

blocks.html: Ordering embroidered kit for a team? Placement, thread colours and wash-grade all get decided up front — talk to us before the garments are made, not after.

faq.q: How do you wash clothes with embroidered logos?
faq.a: Inside out with fastenings closed, at 40 °C on a normal cycle, with standard detergent — no bleach, no softener. Line-dry or tumble cool, and never iron directly over the stitching. The inside-out habit alone prevents most embroidery wear.

faq.q: Why is my printed logo cracking and peeling?
faq.a: Heat. Hot washes and hot tumble-drying soften the transfer adhesive and the film itself; edges lift, then folds crack. Wash at 40 °C, dry cool, and never iron across the print — pressed correctly, a quality transfer lasts years of weekly washing.

faq.q: Is embroidery or printing better for workwear?
faq.a: Embroidery for anything washed hard and often — polos, sweats, fleeces — because stitching outlasts film. Print for waterproof shells (stitching makes needle holes through the membrane), large designs, and fine detail. Many uniforms sensibly use both across the wardrobe.

faq.q: Can you embroider hi-vis and FR workwear?
faq.a: Yes, with rules: on hi-vis the decoration must not encroach on the certified fluorescent background or tape areas, and on FR garments the threads and process must be FR-compatible. That's why branding safety kit should go through the workwear supplier rather than a generic print shop.

pages.cardTitle: Washing FR workwear without killing it
pages.cardBlurb: Flame resistance survives washing only if you follow three prohibitions — softener, bleach and contamination.
pages.h1: Washing FR workwear without washing out the F and the R.
pages.metaTitle: Washing FR Workwear: The Rules That Preserve Flame Resistance | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to launder flame-resistant clothing — why fabric softener and bleach are banned, how treated and inherent FR age differently, the contamination problem, and when FR kit must retire.
pages.lede: Flame-resistant clothing fails silently: a garment that's been washed wrong looks identical to one that will save your skin. The laundering rules exist because two everyday products — fabric softener and bleach — and one everyday substance — the oil the garment picked up at work — can defeat certification the label still claims.

heroMeta.l: Oily FR is a wick, not a shield

steps.name: Wash to the label, separately from non-FR kit
steps.text: Use the temperature and cycle the garment's label states, in a load of FR garments only — household items shed lint and residues onto FR fabric.

steps.name: Use plain detergent — never softener, never chlorine bleach
steps.text: Fabric softener deposits a waxy, flammable film that acts as fuel; chlorine bleach chemically strips FR treatments and degrades aramids. Both are prohibited on effectively every FR label.

steps.name: Remove oil and grease properly
steps.text: Pre-treat hydrocarbon contamination with a degreaser and rewash — an FR garment loaded with oil burns regardless of its certification, because the contamination is fuel the fabric can't refuse.

steps.name: Rinse well, dry per label
steps.text: Detergent residue itself degrades performance over time. Tumble only if the label allows, at the stated heat — over-drying ages treated cottons fast.

steps.name: Inspect and count
steps.text: Check for thinning, tears, contamination that won't lift, and repairs done in non-FR thread or patches. Treated-FR garments have finite wash lives — track them.

blocks.h2: Treated and inherent FR age differently
blocks.html:
The washing rules hit the two FR families differently — the split our inherent vs treated guide covers in full. Treated FR (cotton with a flame-retardant finish) is the wash-sensitive one: the treatment is consumed gradually by laundering and rapidly by chlorine bleach, and manufacturers state a wash-life — commonly 50 washes or more — after which certification lapses whatever the garment looks like. Inherent FR (aramids, modacrylics) can't wash out — the polymer itself is flame-resistant — but softener contamination still coats it with fuel, and physical wear still retires it.

Industrial laundering with FR-compatible processes is the gold standard for treated garments precisely because it controls chemistry and counts cycles; home laundering is workable if the three prohibitions are actually observed — which needs telling people, not just assuming.

blocks.h2: Do and don't, on one screen
head: Do
Don't
rows: Wash FR with FR, to the label
Mix with household laundry or lint-shedding fleece
Use fabric softener — ever, on any FR garment
Pre-treat oil with a degreaser and rewash
Chlorine-bleach stains out of treated cotton
Repair with FR thread and FR patches
Sew ordinary patches over protective fabric
Assume a clean-looking garment is still certified

items.l: Treated garments past their stated wash-life are workwear, not PPE
Contamination that survives degreasing makes the garment a wick — retire it
FR performance assumes intact fabric weight; holes and thinning void the maths

faq.q: Why can't you use fabric softener on FR clothing?
faq.a: Softener deposits a waxy film on fibres that is itself flammable — it effectively coats flame-resistant fabric with fuel, and it builds up wash after wash. Every FR care label prohibits it; it's the most common way good FR kit gets quietly compromised at home.

faq.q: How many times can FR clothing be washed?
faq.a: Inherent FR (aramid, modacrylic) has no wash limit — the fibre itself is flame-resistant for the garment's physical life. Treated FR cotton carries a manufacturer-stated wash-life, often 50 industrial washes or more, after which the certification no longer holds. The label or datasheet states it; someone should be counting.

faq.q: Can FR workwear be washed at home?
faq.a: Usually yes, within the label's rules: FR-only loads, plain detergent, no softener, no chlorine bleach, proper degreasing of oil contamination, and drying to the label. Industrial laundering remains the safer option for treated FR because it controls the chemistry and counts the washes — for hydrocarbon-site kit, many employers mandate it.

pages.cardBlurb: Emulsion, gloss and two-pack behave like three different substances — the removal playbook, and when to stop trying.
pages.h1: Paint on workwear: what comes out, what won't.
pages.metaTitle: Getting Paint Out Of Workwear: Emulsion, Gloss & 2-Pack | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Paint stain removal for workwear — wet emulsion vs dried, oil-based gloss and solvents, why two-pack is permanent, and the painter's honest economics of whites as consumables.
pages.lede: Paint removal has one law: the chemistry of the paint decides everything. Water-based emulsion caught wet rinses out; the same splash dried is a plastic film gripping the weave; and cured two-pack laughs at every product in the cupboard. Knowing which battle you're in saves the wasted hour.

steps.name: Identify the paint before touching it
steps.text: Water-based (emulsion, most trade wall paints), oil-based (gloss, undercoat), or catalysed (two-pack, epoxies). The tin tells you; the removal method follows entirely from this.

steps.name: Wet water-based paint: rinse now
steps.text: Cold running water from the back of the fabric, then wash normally. Speed is everything — emulsion is easy for about an hour and nearly impossible once cured.

steps.name: Dried water-based paint: soften and scrape
steps.text: Warm soapy water soak, then work the film with a blunt edge; repeat. Alcohol-based products help on stubborn films. Expect partial success on textured weaves.

steps.name: Oil-based paint: solvent, outside, sparingly
steps.text: White spirit on a cloth from the fabric's reverse, blotting not rubbing, outdoors — then wash the garment hot with strong detergent to lift the solvent residue. Never machine-wash a solvent-soaked garment directly.

steps.name: Two-pack and epoxies: don't bother
steps.text: Once catalysed, it's a thermoset plastic bonded to the fibres. Nothing that removes it leaves fabric behind. Pick off what lifts, call the rest decoration.

blocks.html:
The trade already knows this: painters' whites are bought expecting decoration — the splatter pattern is practically a CV — and the working economics favour rotation over rescue: enough sets that a paint-heavy day doesn't force a re-wear (the sets maths), removal effort spent only on the big misses, and retirement when stiffness, not stains, says so. A paint-loaded garment that's gone board-stiff has lost its flex and its comfort; that's the replacement signal.

Two cautions from the solvent step: white spirit and fabric softener share a failure mode — residues left in fabric — so post-solvent garments get a hot, thorough wash on their own; and solvent work near FR garments is a hard no — contamination compromises the protection, and FR kit with paint jobs goes through the employer's process, not the utility-room experiment.

head: Paint
Fresh
Dried
rows: Cold rinse + normal wash — near-total success
Soak, scrape, repeat — partial at best
White spirit blot, then hot wash
Wipe the worst before it cures
As emulsion, but the grit shreds success
Blot immediately; success varies by dye

faq.q: How do you get dried emulsion out of clothes?
faq.a: Soak in warm soapy water to soften the film, then work it loose with a blunt edge and repeat — alcohol-based products help stubborn patches. Expect partial success: dried emulsion is a plastic film in the weave, and textured fabrics hold it hardest. Fresh emulsion, by contrast, rinses out almost completely.

faq.q: Does white spirit damage clothing?
faq.a: Used sparingly and washed out properly, usually not — but it must be blotted from the fabric's reverse, used outdoors, and followed by a hot, thorough wash to remove residue. Never put a solvent-wet garment straight into a machine, and never use solvents on FR clothing.

faq.q: Can you remove two-pack paint from workwear?
faq.a: Honestly, no — once catalysed it's a thermoset plastic bonded into the fibres, and anything aggressive enough to attack it destroys the fabric. Wipe splashes before they cure; after that, it's permanent and the garment's future is cosmetic.

pages.cardBlurb: Cement doesn't stain — it cures, and it burns. The removal window, the washing rules and the skin warning that matters more.
pages.h1: Cement on workwear: cure, corrosion and the clock.
pages.metaTitle: Cement & Concrete Stains On Workwear: Removal & Care | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Cement and concrete on workwear — why wet cement is a chemical burn hazard first, the removal window before it cures, machine-washing rules (grit kills machines), and when trousers are done.
pages.lede: Cement isn't a stain — it's a chemical reaction wearing your trousers as a mould. Wet, it's caustic enough to burn skin through soaked fabric; cured, it's rock bonded to the weave. Both facts matter more than laundry technique, which is why this guide starts with the skin and ends with the washing machine.

heroMeta.l: Wet cement is caustic — skin first
What concrete does to washing machines

steps.name: Soaked-through fabric comes off — for the skin, not the garment
steps.text: Wet cement against skin causes alkaline burns that don't hurt until damage is done. Trousers soaked at the knee mean change and rinse the skin now — the classic injury is kneeling in screed all afternoon.

steps.name: Scrape and shake dry material before any water
steps.text: Brush off powder and lumps outside. Dry cement plus water starts curing — don't make paste in the fabric.

steps.name: Rinse splashes cold, soon
steps.text: Fresh mortar and concrete splash rinses out under cold running water within the working hours before initial set. This is the whole removal window.

steps.name: Cured spots: mechanical, not chemical
steps.text: Flex the fabric, pick and brush what cracks free. Acid-based patio cleaners that dissolve concrete also eat dyes and cellulose — they're for slabs, not trousers.

steps.name: Wash grit-heavy kit with mercy on the machine
steps.text: Shake out thoroughly, rinse first, use a bag or a launderette machine for the truly loaded — concrete fines are what kill domestic pumps and bearings.

blocks.h2: Trousers as consumables, skin as the asset
blocks.html:
Groundworkers and formworkers retire trousers the way painters retire whites — by stiffness and abrasion, not stains. Cement-crusted fabric loses flex, chafes, and grinds itself apart at the knees; the working answer is rotation depth, knee protection that spares the fabric (EN 14404 inserts take the kneeling), and acceptance that a season of concrete work consumes cloth. Waterproof over-trousers for pour days are cheaper than trousers.

The skin point deserves its repetition: cement burns are slow-notice injuries — alkaline attack numbs as it damages, and kneeling in fresh screed through ordinary trousers is the textbook case. Wet-work days want waterproof knee cover or wellingtons and gauntlets at the mixing end. Fabric is replaceable.

head: State
Action
Odds
rows: Flex, crack, pick — accept the rest
Garment off, skin rinsed — burns first

faq.q: How do you get cement out of clothes?
faq.a: Dry: brush it off outside before water touches it. Fresh and wet: rinse under cold running water before it sets — that window of a few hours is your whole chance. Cured: mechanical removal only (flex and pick); the acids that dissolve concrete destroy fabric too.

faq.q: Can wet cement burn you through clothing?
faq.a: Yes — fabric soaked with wet cement holds the caustic mix against skin, and alkaline burns develop painlessly over hours. Kneeling in fresh screed is the classic injury. Soaked garments come off promptly and skin gets rinsed thoroughly; wet-work days call for waterproof layers.

faq.q: Does concrete damage washing machines?
faq.a: The grit does — sand and cement fines destroy pumps and bearings. Shake and brush kit outside, pre-rinse heavily loaded garments, and consider a dedicated or launderette machine for the worst. Never wash chunks of cured concrete through a domestic drum.

pages.cardBlurb: The overnight-dry problem solved — what tumble heat ruins, what damp kit costs, and the drying-room logic that works at home.
pages.metaTitle: Drying Workwear Properly: Tumble Rules & Overnight Drying | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to dry workwear properly — which garments tumble and which die in the dryer, the overnight drying setup that actually works, boot drying without cracking, and why damp kit is a health issue.
pages.lede: The hardest workwear problem in Britain isn't washing — it's Tuesday night: soaked kit, a 6am start, and a tumble dryer that ruins half of what goes in it. Drying is where good garments die young and where damp ones quietly become a health issue, so it deserves the ten minutes of system the trade rarely gives it.

heroMeta.l: The real answer to wet Tuesdays

blocks.html:
The dryer's casualty list is long and specific: waterproof membranes and taped seams delaminate (unless the label explicitly allows low tumble — some DWR revival actually wants it, label first); elastane-rich stretch fabrics lose their snap; prints and transfers crack; hi-vis fades faster (the compliance angle); FR garments follow their label exactly (the FR rules); and anything still stained gets its stain heat-set permanently. What tumbles happily: cotton-rich tees, sweats, polycotton trousers without stretch, towelling. The label knows; the habit doesn't ask.

The overnight system that works without a dryer is a drying room shrunk to a corner: garments spaced on hangers (not heaped on a radiator), moving air from a cheap fan doing more than heat ever does, modest background warmth, and ideally a dehumidifier — which dries kit faster than a radiator and doesn't wallpaper the room with condensation. Boots get their own rule: insoles out, newspaper or a boot dryer, never the radiator top — direct heat cracks leather and delaminates soles, which is how wet boots become dead boots in one winter.

faq.q: Can you tumble dry work trousers?
faq.a: Plain polycotton trousers usually yes, on the label's setting — but stretch (elastane) content, waterproof membranes and knee-pad pocket linings often say no or low. Check each garment's label once and sort loads accordingly; one hot load ruins stretch recovery permanently.

faq.q: How do you dry workwear overnight without a dryer?
faq.a: Space garments on hangers, add moving air (a basic fan) and modest warmth, ideally with a dehumidifier — airflow dries faster than radiator heat and doesn't condense on the windows. Heaped-on-radiator drying is slow and cooks the contact points.

faq.q: How do you dry wet work boots?
faq.a: Insoles out, laces loosened, stuffed with newspaper (changed once) or on a boot dryer — never on or against a radiator, which cracks leather and delaminates soles. Overnight is usually enough with airflow; two pairs in rotation is the winter answer.

pages.cardBlurb: UV, damp and van floors age kit faster than work does — seasonal storage, PPE shelf lives and the van-as-wardrobe problem.
pages.h1: Storing kit: where garments go to age.
pages.metaTitle: Storing Workwear & PPE: Shelf Life, UV & Van Storage | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: How to store workwear and PPE — seasonal storage that doesn't ruin garments, PPE shelf lives (helmets, respirators, gloves), the van rear-window problem, and issue-stock rotation for employers.
pages.lede: Kit ages in storage almost as effectively as in use: UV through a van window chalks a helmet, damp in a February shed mildews a summer wardrobe, and the glovebox FFP mask is a write-off by design. Storage is the unglamorous half of making kit last — and for PPE, some of it has rules.

heroMeta.l: The two words of seasonal storage

blocks.html:
Seasonal garment storage is two words: clean and dry. Wash everything before it goes away (body oils and soiling set, attract moths and feed mildew over months), dry it completely (the drying rules apply doubly before storage), and box it somewhere dry rather than bagging it airtight while any moisture remains. Reproof waterproofs at the start of storage, not in the October panic — the routine — and store FR kit clean, because stored contamination is still contamination.

PPE adds shelf lives. Helmets age from manufacture, worn or not (check the stamp); disposable respirators carry expiry dates and die early in damp glovebox conditions; glove polymers stiffen and crack in van heat cycles; and retroreflective tape on stored hi-vis delaminates in damp. The van deserves its own paragraph because it's where trade kit actually lives: the rear window ledge is a UV oven (fading hi-vis and chalking helmets parked in plain sight), the wet-kit heap in the back grows what wet heaps grow, and the answer costs little — kit bags or boxes, off the glass, spare gloves and masks in sealed tubs, wet gear separated until it dries. For employers, stock storage is rotation: first-in-first-out on dated PPE, and issue stores kept dry enough that the stock isn't ageing faster than it's issued — the records logic extends to the shelf.

head: Item
Storage rule
The killer
rows: Washed, bone dry, boxed in the dry
Cool, dark, off the parcel shelf

faq.q: How should you store workwear over summer or winter?
faq.a: Washed, completely dried, and boxed or hung somewhere dry — soiling set over months attracts moths and mildew, and trapped moisture ruins more stored kit than moths do. Reproof waterproofs before storage rather than after, and store FR clean as a rule.

faq.q: Does PPE expire in storage?
faq.a: Much of it ages regardless of use: helmet shells date from manufacture, disposable respirators carry expiry dates, and glove polymers stiffen with heat cycles. Store PPE cool, dry and dark, rotate stock first-in-first-out, and check date stamps at issue.

faq.q: Is it bad to keep workwear in the van?
faq.a: The van is fine as a wardrobe and terrible as a shelf: UV through windows fades hi-vis and degrades helmets, damp heaps mildew, and gloveboxes kill masks. Boxes off the glass, sealed tubs for spares and separating wet kit until dry fixes almost all of it.

pages.cardTitle: Repair or replace: the workwear triage
pages.cardBlurb: What's worth stitching, what's structurally done, and the PPE rule: protection is never patched back on.
pages.h1: Repair or replace: triage for tired kit.
pages.metaTitle: Repair Or Replace Workwear: The Honest Triage | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: When to repair workwear and when to retire it — seams and zips vs structural wear, the PPE rule (certified performance is never patched back), and the fleet economics of repair programmes.
pages.lede: Somewhere between the ripped knee that's one stitch from fine and the coverall that's more oil than cotton sits a triage decision every trade makes weekly. The sorting logic is short: hardware and seams repair well, structure doesn't, and certified protection — once compromised — is never sewn back on.

blocks.html:
Repair with confidence: failed hardware and stitching — zips, poppers, buttons, opened seams, dropped hems, torn belt loops. These are assembly failures, not fabric failures, and a repair restores full function; on quality garments a zip replacement is money well spent. Clean tears in sound fabric (the fence-hook rip) also patch well — iron-on backing plus stitching, or proper trade repair patches on knees and elbows of non-certified kit.

Retire without sentiment: structural wear — fabric thinned at seat and knees (hold it to the light), abrasion fuzzing through, elastane gone slack, or contamination that survives proper washing: the oil-saturated coverall, the board-stiff trouser. Repairing thin fabric is stitching a patch to tissue; the next tear is already queued beside it.

The PPE rule sits above both buckets: certified performance is never patched back on. Damaged hi-vis can't have tape re-stuck; FR garments repair only through FR-competent services with FR materials — a cotton patch on FR fabric is a wick; and chainsaw layers, impacted helmets and spent knee inserts replace, full stop. If the garment's job was certified protection and that protection is compromised, the triage has one bucket.

faq.q: Is it worth repairing work trousers?
faq.a: For hardware and seam failures on decent trousers, yes — zips, poppers and opened seams repair to full function. For fabric thinned at the knees and seat, no: patches stitched to weakened cloth relocate the next tear rather than preventing it. The light test (hold it up, look through) settles most cases.

faq.q: Can you repair hi-vis clothing?
faq.a: Minor seam repairs away from the tape, perhaps — but damaged or delaminating retroreflective tape and heavily faded fluorescent fabric can't be restored, and the garment no longer meets its certified class. Hi-vis is retired on visibility condition, not stitched onward.

faq.q: Can FR workwear be patched?
faq.a: Only through FR-competent repair using matching FR fabrics and threads — an ordinary cotton or polyester patch on FR clothing creates a flammable island on a protective garment. Many employers route FR repairs through their laundering/rental service or simply replace; casual patching is the one wrong answer.

pages.cardBlurb: Wash counts, fade tests and the six-month myth — when high-visibility kit genuinely stops being high-visibility.
pages.metaTitle: How Long Does Hi-Vis Last? Lifespan & Replacement Signs | iNeedWorkwear
pages.metaDesc: Hi-vis lifespan answered — what maximum wash counts mean, the visual checks that beat any calendar (fade, grey tape, delamination), and how use patterns change garment life from months to years.
pages.lede: There's no expiry date sewn into a hi-vis vest — but there is a wash-count on the label, a fade test anyone can do in daylight, and a set of use patterns that stretch identical garments from three months of life to three years. Here's how the lifespan question actually resolves.

heroMeta.l: Compare against new — fade is obvious

blocks.html:
Clock one: the wash count. Hi-vis labels state a maximum number of wash cycles (commonly 25, often 50 on better garments) — the point up to which the fluorescent dye and retroreflective tape are warranted to keep certified performance if washed correctly (the washing rules). Nobody counts domestic washes, which is why the second clock matters more.

Clock two: visible condition. Fluorescence fades toward ordinary yellow-green (hold it beside a new garment in daylight — the difference announces itself), tape greys, cracks or delaminates at the flex lines, and soiling that washing won't lift kills both properties at once. Any of those means the garment no longer delivers its class, whatever its age. Clock three: exposure. UV is the ager — a garment worn daily outdoors (or stored on a van shelf) fades in months; the same garment on occasional indoor duty lasts years; coastal salt air accelerates everything. The honest answer to 'how long': daily outdoor wear, expect 6–12 months; occasional use, 2–3 years; and the daylight comparison overrules both.

head: Check
Fail looks like
rows: Washed-out, ordinary-looking yellow — the fluorescence is gone
Grey, cracked, peeling at flex points — or dull under headlights
Ground-in grime the wash can't lift, especially across tape
Tears, burns or repairs through fluorescent area or tape
Wash count exceeded, or label illegible (traceability gone)

faq.q: How often should hi-vis be replaced?
faq.a: On condition, not calendar: daily outdoor wearers typically get 6–12 months before fade or tape wear retires a garment; occasional users can see years. The reliable test is comparing against a new garment in daylight — visible fade means the certified performance is gone.

faq.q: What does the wash count on hi-vis mean?
faq.a: The maximum number of care-label washes for which the maker warrants certified performance — commonly 25 to 50. Beyond it (or after incorrect washing: hot cycles, tumble heat) the fluorescent dye and tape can no longer be assumed to meet the class, however intact the garment looks.

faq.q: Does hi-vis fade in sunlight?
faq.a: Yes — UV exposure is the main ager of fluorescent dye, working on the garment whether it's being worn or parked on a van's rear shelf. Store hi-vis out of sunlight, wash it cool, line-dry it, and it keeps its class for the full wash-count instead of dying early.
